summary: Natalie Zemon Davis becomes a full person entry. Her description, works, scope and chronology are rewritten from read texts: ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973), her Haskins Lecture (1997), Finlay’s critique and her reply (1988), Stone (1979), Scott (1986), with Thompson (1972), her AHA address (1987), the Holberg committee (2010) and memorials (2023–24). Twelve edges: contributions to gender, women’s history, cultural history, social history, microhistory, the narrative debate and global history; influences from Thompson, anthropology and Bloch, and her influence on Thompson; Finlay’s critique (micro → Davis). Chronology: 16 dated contributions (1966–2010, the 1982 film and French book apart), her 1997 retrospect on the context track, two editions (1983 English book; 1988 printing of her AHA address) and nine reception events. Roster: six existing rows revised; new rows on gender, global, annales and public history, and Finlay as critic in microhistory. Two new strands (micro/reconstruction_invention; women/early_modern_sexes). Edges 005 and 040 distinguish her acknowledged Geertz reading from any specific adoption. The biography claim is accepted on read body text and edge_755 loses its provisional label. Her general bibliography lists 28 sources.

rationale: Davis had one provisional edge (to biography, from a book description) and a single 1995 timeline point, while six roster rows and several group edges already named her. The research read her own texts (‘Rites of Violence’, 1973, in part; the 1997 Haskins Lecture in full; ‘On the Lame’, 1988, in part), Finlay (1988) in full, Stone (1979) and Scott (1986) at the relevant pages, the Holberg committee statement in full, and Thompson (1972), her AHA address (1987), Hesse (2024) and Fossett (2001) in tool-limited excerpts. Each edge rests on her acknowledgement or a named reader’s explicit statement; mediated and retrospective claims are labelled as such. Unread works (Martin Guerre, Fiction in the Archives, The Gift, Slaves on Screen, Trickster Travels) supply bibliographic dates and mediated interpretations, each attributed to her retrospect or a named reader; Estèbe 1975, Ginzburg 1984, Desan 1989 and the Walsham letters are not used beyond titles. Her node’s source_ids are extended to the full bibliography; work_ids and claim_ids are unchanged. Reviewed by Sol (release/sol-review-1.143.md, accept with fixes); all twelve fixes are recorded in release/fixes-1.143.md.

edge_755.evidence_note: 1.119 assessment, superseded in revision 1.143: ‘Davis connects three contrasting lives with religious, social and colonial settings. Description supports the proposed comparative-biography scope; body-text verification remains outstanding.’ Revision 1.143: the body text is read for this claim. The graph’s primary selection (davis_margins_primary: prologue pp. 1–4, conclusion pp. 203–216, acknowledgments pp. 340–344; read 2026-09-12) shows an explicitly imagined prologue, not testimony, and a conclusion that compares the three women while keeping religious difference and colonial domination in view. Her 1997 Haskins Lecture (read in full): ‘I would expand the single microhistory into a decentered comparison of three European lives’ (p. 21); ‘All three of these women were on margins, religious, social, geographical … All three turned these margins into borderlands for discovery’ (p. 22). Main chapters remain unread. No new Certeau/Foucault borrowing or narrative-revival influence is inferred. The target is the named strand, displayed under its parent entry.

text_revisions.old: Uses contrasting seventeenth-century lives to investigate religion, writing and relations of power across Europe and its colonial outposts. Women on the Margins makes individual lives a route into broader historical questions.
text_revisions.new: A historian of sixteenth-century France whose work moved from the social history of Lyon’s printing workers to ritual, gender, storytelling and lives that crossed religious and colonial borders. By her own account (1997) she ‘combined archival work with the study of printed texts of multiple genres’, and Laurie Nussdorfer’s memorial calls her ‘the rare social historian who valued printed sources’. In ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973) she argued that religious riot drew on ‘a store of punitive or purificatory traditions’ and had ‘a connection in time, place and form with the life of worship’, so that such violence was ‘related here less to the pathological than to the normal’; she explicitly distinguished explaining the ritual structure of violence from granting a right to commit it: ‘the rites of violence are not the rights of violence in any absolute sense’. She acknowledged the crowd histories of Rudé, Hobsbawm, Thompson and Tilly and applied Thompson’s account of the food riot’s legitimation to the religious crowd. By her own account she came to ritual through Van Gennep’s folklore and read Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz ‘eclectically … not looking for solutions, but for questions’ (1997); Thompson, for his part, called her charivari essay ‘une étude importante’ (1972). Joan Scott (1986) quoted her call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ as an early relational use of gender, and with Jill Conway she taught in 1971 what she called ‘the first course in women’s history in Canada’. In 1997 she said she came to microhistory, ‘or what I called ethnography’, through the film of Martin Guerre, on whose script she worked; her book followed in French (1982) and English (1983). Robert Finlay (1988) charged that she had ‘permitted an excess of invention’ against ‘the sovereignty of the sources’; she answered that where reconstruction stops and invention begins was ‘precisely the question I hoped readers would ask’. In her 1997 retrospect she described the ‘fiction’ of Fiction in the Archives (1987) as ‘the crafting element’, not falsification, and Women on the Margins (1995) as ‘a decentered comparison’ of three lives, whose conclusion keeps religious difference and colonial domination in view. The Holberg committee (2010) described The Gift (2000) as illuminating ‘the intricate forms of pre-market exchange and reciprocity’, Slaves on Screen (2000) as dealing with ‘the alteration of historical material in contemporary film’ and Trickster Travels (2006), with Women on the Margins, as exploring ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’; it saw her uniqueness in ‘connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history’.

text_revisions.new: Natalie Zemon Davis (1928–2023); dissertation on Lyon’s Protestants and printing workers (1959); “A Trade Union in Sixteenth-Century France” (Economic History Review, 1966); “The Reasons of Misrule: Youth Groups and Charivaris in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1971); “The Rites of Violence: Religious Riot in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1973; reprinted in Society and Culture in Early Modern France, 1975); “‘Women’s History’ in Transition: The European Case” (Feminist Studies, 1976; quoted by Scott, 1986); Le Retour de Martin Guerre (Paris: Robert Laffont, 1982; the catalogue record also credits Jean-Claude Carrière and Daniel Vigne, scenarist and director of the 1982 film on whose script she worked) and The Return of Martin Guerre (Harvard, 1983); “History’s Two Bodies” (AHA presidential address, 1987; AHR 1988); Fiction in the Archives: Pardon Tales and Their Tellers in Sixteenth-Century France (1987); “On the Lame” (AHR Forum, 1988, reply to Finlay); Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995); A Life of Learning (Haskins Lecture, 1997); Slaves on Screen: Film and Historical Vision (2000); The Gift in Sixteenth-Century France (2000); Trickster Travels: A Sixteenth-Century Muslim between Worlds (2006); “Decentering History” (Holberg Symposium, 2010); later titles named in Nussdorfer’s memorial (unread): Leo Africanus Discovers Comedy: Theatre and Poetry Across the Mediterranean (2021) and Listening to the Languages of the People: Lazare Sainéan on Romanian, Yiddish and French (2022). Readers and critics: E. P. Thompson (1972); Lawrence Stone (1979); Joan Scott (1986); Robert Finlay (1988); Lynn Hunt, ed., with Suzanne Desan’s chapter (1989); Judith Jackson Fossett (2001); Holberg Prize committee (2010); Alexandra Walsham (2017); Laurie Nussdorfer (2023); Carla Hesse (2024).

text_revisions.old: Comparative biography provides a connection beyond gender history. This entry is supported by a newly checked book description; its methodological interpretation still needs a fresh body-text check. Other career contributions remain in the preserved contexts.
text_revisions.new: Read for revision 1.143: ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973), pp. 52–53, 57, 60–61 and 90–91; her Haskins Lecture, A Life of Learning (1997), in full, cited as her later account of her course, not as evidence of what the earlier works say; ‘On the Lame’ (1988), pp. 572, 574–576, 584, 587, 600 and 602–603; Finlay’s critique (1988) in full; Stone (1979), pp. 3 and 18; Scott (1986), p. 1054; and, earlier, the prologue, conclusion and acknowledgments of Women on the Margins. Thompson’s ‘Rough Music’ (1972, by paragraph in a 2020 reprint), her AHA address (1987) and the AHA memorial (2024) are read only in short excerpts. The Return of Martin Guerre, Fiction in the Archives, The Gift, Slaves on Screen, Trickster Travels and the 2021–22 books are unread: they supply bibliographic dates and mediated interpretations only, given in her own retrospect or in named readers’ words (the Holberg committee, Fossett, Finlay, Nussdorfer). Also unread: ‘Women’s History in Transition’ (1976; her words as Scott quotes them), Estèbe’s 1975 comment on ‘Rites’ and her rejoinder, Ginzburg’s 1984 postface to the Italian Martin Guerre, Desan’s 1989 chapter and the Davis–Thompson letters (Walsham 2017; opening only). She is not presented as the founder of microhistory, cultural history or gender history: by her own account Le Roy Ladurie and Ginzburg reached microhistory by other routes, Scott quotes her as one relational voice among others, and anthropology supplied questions tested on ‘only historical evidence’. Finlay’s charge of invention and her reply are both kept, as is Fossett’s criticism (2001) that Slaves on Screen ‘raises more questions than it answers’. Not to be confused with J. C. Davis (the Ranter debate) or Donald F. Davis (Canadian urban history).

strand.title: Reconstruction, invention and the sovereignty of sources
strand.focus: In ‘On the Lame’ (1988) Davis described her reconstruction of a village imposture from legal, notarial and printed records as conjectural, citing Ginzburg’s evidential paradigm; Finlay contests where reconstruction becomes invention, and Davis replies that the boundary was the book’s question. Both positions are recorded; neither settles the method.
